question: Under Rule 2 (Responsibility) of the Inland Navigation Rules, does complying with the specific right-of-way rules ever excuse an operator from the consequences of poor seamanship?
choice_a: Yes, following the specific rules is always a complete defense no matter what happens
choice_b: No -- nothing in the Rules exonerates a vessel or its operator from the consequences of neglecting ordinary seamanship precautions or the special circumstances of the case
choice_c: This requirement applies only to licensed commercial captains, not recreational boaters
choice_d: This rule applies only after a collision has already occurred
explanation: Rule 2 is the general 'prudential rule': nothing in the Navigation Rules excuses a vessel or its owner, master, or crew from neglecting ordinary seamanship precautions or the special circumstances of the case, and departure from the Rules is only justified to avoid immediate danger.

question: Under the Inland Navigation Rules, when is a vessel considered to be 'underway'?
choice_a: Only when its engine is running
choice_b: Whenever it is drifting with no one aboard
choice_c: Whenever it is not at anchor, made fast to the shore, or aground
choice_d: Only when it is moving faster than idle speed
explanation: Rule 3 defines 'underway' as meaning that a vessel is not at anchor, made fast to the shore, or aground -- a drifting vessel with its engine off is still legally underway.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.03, Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 3 (General Definitions)

question: Under the Inland Navigation Rules, what is the difference between a 'vessel not under command' and a 'vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver'?
choice_a: There is no difference -- the two terms mean exactly the same thing
choice_b: A vessel not under command is always a sailing vessel
choice_c: A vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver is always less than 20 meters long
choice_d: A vessel not under command is unable to maneuver due to some exceptional circumstance, such as a mechanical failure, while a vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver is limited by the nature of the work she is doing
explanation: Rule 3 defines a 'vessel not under command' as one unable to maneuver as required by the Rules due to some exceptional circumstance, while a 'vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver' is one whose nature of work limits her maneuverability, such as a vessel laying cable or engaged in dredging.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.03, Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 3 (General Definitions)

question: Under Rule 6 (Safe Speed), which of the following must every vessel operator consider when choosing a safe operating speed?
choice_a: The state of visibility, traffic density, and the vessel's maneuverability, including stopping distance and turning ability
choice_b: Only the posted speed limit signs visible from shore
choice_c: Only whether other boaters can read the vessel's registration numbers
choice_d: Safe speed requirements apply only to vessels over 26 feet in length
explanation: Rule 6 requires every vessel to proceed at a safe speed so it can take proper and effective action to avoid collision, considering factors such as visibility, traffic density, maneuverability and stopping distance, background lighting at night, wind/sea/current conditions, and draft in relation to water depth.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.06, Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 6 (Safe Speed)

question: Under Rule 7 (Risk of Collision), how can an operator recognize that risk of collision exists with an approaching vessel?
choice_a: Risk of collision only exists once the two vessels are within 50 feet of each other
choice_b: Risk of collision is deemed to exist if the compass bearing to the approaching vessel does not appreciably change over time
choice_c: Risk of collision exists only during periods of restricted visibility
choice_d: Risk of collision can always be ruled out if the other vessel is a sailboat
explanation: Rule 7 states that risk of collision shall be deemed to exist if the compass bearing of an approaching vessel does not appreciably change, and warns that assumptions should never be made on the basis of scanty information, especially scanty radar information.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.07, Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 7 (Risk of Collision)

question: Under Rule 8 (Action to Avoid Collision), what must an alteration of course or speed made to avoid a collision be like?
choice_a: As small and gradual as possible so the other operator does not notice the change
choice_b: Made only at the very last possible moment to avoid overreacting
choice_c: Large enough to be readily apparent to the other vessel, made in ample time, and result in passing at a safe distance
choice_d: A change in course only -- speed may never be changed to avoid a collision
explanation: Rule 8 requires that any course or speed alteration to avoid collision be large enough to be readily apparent to another vessel observing visually or by radar, and be taken in ample time so the vessels pass at a safe distance -- small, tentative changes are exactly what the rule warns against.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.08, Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 8 (Action to Avoid Collision)

question: If necessary to avoid a collision or to allow more time to assess a developing situation, what does Rule 8 direct a vessel operator to do?
choice_a: Immediately accelerate away from the other vessel regardless of surroundings
choice_b: Shut off all engines and drift, regardless of the situation
choice_c: Sound the danger signal and continue on the same course and speed
choice_d: Slacken her speed or take all way off (come to a stop) as needed
explanation: Rule 8(e) provides that if necessary to avoid collision or to allow more time to assess the situation, a vessel shall slacken her speed or take all way off by stopping or reversing her means of propulsion.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.08, Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 8 (Action to Avoid Collision)

question: Under Rule 9 (Narrow Channels), where should a vessel generally keep while proceeding along a narrow channel or fairway?
choice_a: As near to the outer limit of the channel that lies on her own starboard side as is safe and practicable
choice_b: In the exact center of the channel at all times, regardless of other traffic
choice_c: As near to the outer limit on her port side as is safe and practicable
choice_d: Wherever avoids the strongest current, regardless of which side of the channel that is
explanation: Rule 9(a) requires a vessel proceeding along a narrow channel or fairway to keep as near to the outer limit of the channel that lies on her own starboard side as is safe and practicable, similar to keeping to the right on a road.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.09, Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 9 (Narrow Channels)

question: What must a vessel operator do when approaching a bend or an obstructed area of a narrow channel where other vessels may be hidden from view?
choice_a: Automatically sound the danger signal of five or more short, rapid blasts
choice_b: Navigate with particular alertness and caution and sound one prolonged blast on the whistle
choice_c: Increase speed to clear the blind bend before another vessel can arrive
choice_d: No special caution or signal is required if the operator is familiar with the area
explanation: Rule 9(f) requires a vessel nearing a bend or obstructed section of a narrow channel where other vessels may be obscured to navigate with particular alertness and caution and to sound one prolonged blast, which an approaching vessel within hearing should answer with a prolonged blast of her own.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.09, Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 9(f) (Narrow Channels)

question: Under Rule 9 (Narrow Channels), what should a vessel generally avoid doing while transiting a narrow channel, if the circumstances of the case admit?
explanation: Rule 9(g) states that any vessel shall, if the circumstances of the case admit, avoid anchoring in a narrow channel, since an anchored vessel can block or endanger other traffic confined to that channel.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.09, Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 9(g) (Narrow Channels)

question: If a vessel operator is in doubt as to whether they are overtaking another vessel or instead approaching it in a crossing situation, what does Rule 13 direct?
choice_a: The operator should assume the other vessel is automatically the give-way vessel
choice_b: The operator should sound the danger signal and take no further action
choice_c: Doubt has no legal effect, and the operator may proceed however is most convenient
choice_d: The operator shall assume it is an overtaking situation and act accordingly, keeping clear as the give-way vessel
explanation: Rule 13(c) provides that when a vessel is in any doubt as to whether she is overtaking another, she shall assume that she is and act accordingly, keeping out of the way of the vessel ahead.

question: Once one vessel is overtaking another, does a later change in the compass bearing between the two vessels turn the encounter into a crossing situation and relieve the overtaking vessel of her give-way duty?
choice_a: No -- a subsequent change in bearing does not make the overtaking vessel a crossing vessel or relieve her of the duty to keep clear until she is finally past and clear
choice_b: Yes, any change in bearing automatically converts the encounter into a crossing situation
choice_c: Yes, but only if the bearing changes by more than 10 degrees
choice_d: The overtaking vessel's give-way duty only applies for the first minute of the encounter
explanation: Rule 13(d) states that any subsequent alteration of the bearing between the two vessels does not make the overtaking vessel a crossing vessel or relieve her of the duty of keeping clear of the vessel being overtaken until she is finally past and clear.

question: If an operator is in doubt as to whether a head-on situation exists with an approaching power-driven vessel, what does Rule 14 direct the operator to do?
choice_a: Assume no head-on situation exists unless the other vessel sounds a signal first
choice_b: Assume that a head-on situation does exist and act accordingly by altering course to starboard
choice_c: Wait for the other vessel to make the first move before doing anything
choice_d: Only take action if the other vessel is larger than their own boat
explanation: Rule 14(c) provides that when a vessel is in any doubt as to whether a head-on situation exists, she shall assume that it does exist and act accordingly, altering course to starboard as required by Rule 14(a).
source_note: 33 CFR 83.14, Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 14(c) (Head-On Situation)

question: Rule 17 allows a stand-on vessel to take her own action to avoid collision even before an extreme emergency develops. Under what circumstance is this permitted?
choice_a: At any time, for any reason, regardless of what the give-way vessel is doing
choice_b: Only after the two vessels have already collided
choice_c: As soon as it becomes apparent to the stand-on vessel that the give-way vessel is not taking appropriate action to keep clear
choice_d: Never -- the stand-on vessel must hold course and speed no matter what happens
explanation: Rule 17(a)(ii) provides that a stand-on vessel may take action to avoid collision by her own maneuver as soon as it becomes apparent to her that the give-way vessel is not taking appropriate action in compliance with the Rules.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.17, Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 17(a)(ii) (Action by Stand-On Vessel)

question: When a power-driven stand-on vessel finally takes her own action in a crossing situation because the give-way vessel has failed to act, what does Rule 17(c) say she should generally avoid doing, if circumstances allow?
choice_a: Slowing down or stopping her engine
choice_c: Turning on her required navigation lights
choice_d: Altering course to port for a vessel that is on her own port side
explanation: Rule 17(c) provides that a power-driven vessel taking action in a crossing situation under 17(a)(ii) to avoid collision with another power-driven vessel shall, if circumstances admit, not alter course to port for a vessel on her own port side.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.17, Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 17(c) (Action by Stand-On Vessel)

question: Under Rule 18 (Responsibilities Between Vessels), which of the following correctly describes part of the right-of-way priority hierarchy among vessel types?
choice_a: A power-driven vessel underway shall generally keep out of the way of a vessel not under command, a vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver, a vessel engaged in fishing, and a sailing vessel
choice_b: A power-driven vessel always has right-of-way over a sailing vessel, regardless of the circumstances
choice_c: A vessel engaged in fishing must always give way to recreational power boats
choice_d: The Navigation Rules establish no priority order among different types of vessels
explanation: Rule 18 sets a priority order: a power-driven vessel underway must keep out of the way of a vessel not under command, a vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver, a vessel engaged in fishing, and a sailing vessel; sailing vessels and fishing vessels in turn must keep clear of vessels not under command and vessels restricted in their ability to maneuver.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.18, Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 18 (Responsibilities Between Vessels)

question: What does two short blasts of a vessel's horn mean when signaling intentions to a nearby vessel under the Inland Navigation Rules?
choice_b: I intend to leave you on my starboard side (I am altering my course to port)
choice_d: I am at anchor and not under command
explanation: Under Rule 34, two short blasts signal 'I intend to leave you on my starboard side,' meaning the signaling vessel intends to alter course to port.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.34, Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 34 (Maneuvering and Warning Signals)

question: What does three short blasts of a vessel's horn signal to nearby vessels under the Inland Navigation Rules?
choice_a: I intend to leave you on my port side
choice_b: I am the stand-on vessel and will not alter my course
choice_c: I am operating astern propulsion (backing down)
choice_d: I am anchored for the night
explanation: Under Rule 34, three short blasts signal 'I am operating astern propulsion,' alerting nearby vessels that the signaling vessel is backing down.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.34, Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 34 (Maneuvering and Warning Signals)
